scenes.dialogue: Your phone is stolen in another city. Must you go back there to report it? Under the B N S S, you need not.
scenes.shown: Your phone is stolen in another city. Must you go back there to report it? Under the BNSS, you need not.
scenes.chip: 1 · WHERE CAN YOU REPORT A CRIME?

scenes.dialogue: Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. Where, and how, can an F I R be lodged under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita? What if it is not recorded?
scenes.shown: Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. Where, and how, can an FIR be lodged under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita? What if it is not recorded?

scenes.dialogue: Here is a hypothetical. Meera, a teacher from Mysuru, has her phone stolen at a bus stand in Hubballi.
Section One Seventy Three, sub section One, deals with information about a cognizable offence. Once recorded, it is commonly called the F I R.
scenes.shown: Section 173(1) deals with information about a cognizable offence. Once recorded, it is commonly called the FIR.

scenes.dialogue: It may be given in writing, orally, or electronically, to the officer in charge of a police station.
Oral information is reduced to writing, read over to the informant, and signed.
Notice the words: irrespective of the area where the offence is committed. That phrase is the basis of the Zero F I R.
scenes.shown: Notice the words: irrespective of the area where the offence is committed. That phrase is the basis of the Zero FIR.

scenes.dialogue: Assume Meera's information discloses a cognizable offence. She may report it at a police station in Mysuru.
It is recorded there, and the case is then generally transferred to the police station that has jurisdiction.
Under the old Code of Criminal Procedure, the Supreme Court held in Satvinder Kaur that police cannot refuse an F I R only for lack of jurisdiction.
scenes.shown: Under the old Code of Criminal Procedure, the Supreme Court held in Satvinder Kaur that police cannot refuse an FIR only for lack of jurisdiction.

scenes.dialogue: Now suppose Meera reports electronically, from a laptop. That is the E F I R route; the Sanhita calls it electronic communication.
scenes.shown: Now suppose Meera reports electronically, from a laptop. That is the e-FIR route; the Sanhita calls it electronic communication.

scenes.dialogue: Under clause Two, it is taken on record once the person giving it signs it within three days.
scenes.shown: Under clause (ii), it is taken on record once the person giving it signs it within three days.

scenes.dialogue: When a woman reports specified offences against her, such as sexual offences or an acid attack, a woman officer must record it.
If the victim of these offences is disabled, it is recorded at home or a chosen place, with an interpreter or special educator, and videographed.
Under sub section Two, the informant or the victim gets a free copy of the information as recorded, forthwith.
scenes.shown: Under sub-section (2), the informant or the victim gets a free copy of the information as recorded, forthwith.

scenes.dialogue: Under the old Code, the Constitution Bench in Lalita Kumari held registration mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence.
A preliminary inquiry was permitted only in limited cases, and only to check whether a cognizable offence was disclosed.
Sub section Three is new. For offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, police may hold a preliminary enquiry.
scenes.shown: Sub-section (3) is new. For offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, police may hold a preliminary enquiry.

scenes.dialogue: It needs prior permission from a Deputy Superintendent of Police or above, and must check, within fourteen days, whether a prima facie case exists.
scenes.shown: It needs prior permission from a Deputy Superintendent of Police or above, and must check, within 14 days, whether a prima facie case exists.

scenes.dialogue: The Supreme Court has called this an exception, allowing enquiry even when a cognizable offence is disclosed.
Outside that exception, registration remains mandatory. And if the enquiry finds no prima facie case, the informant should be told immediately.
Now suppose the information is not recorded. Section One Seventy Three, sub section Four, gives Meera a remedy.
scenes.shown: Now suppose the information is not recorded. Section 173(4) gives Meera a remedy.

scenes.dialogue: She may send the substance of her information, in writing and by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned.
If satisfied that it discloses a cognizable offence, the Superintendent must investigate, or direct a subordinate officer to investigate.
Failing that, she may apply to the Magistrate. Section One Seventy Five, sub section Three, requires an affidavit in support.
scenes.shown: Failing that, she may apply to the Magistrate. Section 175(3) requires an affidavit in support.

scenes.dialogue: The Magistrate may make any necessary inquiry, and must consider the police officer's submissions, before ordering investigation.
The Supreme Court has said these conditions codify earlier judicial safeguards, like Priyanka Srivastava's affidavit rule under the old Code.
What if the information discloses only a non cognizable offence? Then Section One Seventy Four applies instead.
scenes.shown: What if the information discloses only a non-cognizable offence? Then Section 174 applies instead.

scenes.dialogue: The officer records its substance in a book, and refers the informant to the Magistrate.
Police need a Magistrate's order to investigate it. But where at least one offence is cognizable, the whole case is treated as cognizable.
Registration is not arrest, and an F I R is not proof of guilt; that is for the court.
scenes.shown: Registration is not arrest, and an FIR is not proof of guilt; that is for the court.

scenes.dialogue: Nor is it substantive evidence. It can generally be used only to corroborate or contradict its maker.
Under the old Code, the Supreme Court also held that an F I R is not an encyclopaedia of every fact and detail.
scenes.shown: Under the old Code, the Supreme Court also held that an FIR is not an encyclopaedia of every fact and detail.

scenes.dialogue: Report promptly. Delay is not fatal by itself, but courts look for a satisfactory explanation, because delay can invite embellishment.
Knowingly giving false information may be an offence, for example under Sections Two Seventeen and Two Forty Eight of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
scenes.shown: Knowingly giving false information may be an offence, for example under Sections 217 and 248 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

scenes.dialogue: Finally, a quick checklist. Take your free copy, check that it records your facts accurately, and note the sections mentioned.
Not recorded? Write to the Superintendent of Police by post. If that fails, apply to the Magistrate, with an affidavit and a copy of that letter.
